Expectation1: Attending children's school events and activities
Situation1: The school reports that the child was caught bullying a classmate, and the mother needs to respond
Expectation2: Raise public awareness about social inequities and marginalized groups
Situation2: They respond to an urgent incident of discrimination that requires immediate public attention and awareness.
Story:
I stared at my phone, my heart pounding. The school had called—my son was caught bullying a classmate. The principal wanted me to come in, to talk, to help my child understand the gravity of his actions. As a mother, I felt a wave of shame and worry. My son needed me, needed guidance, and I owed it to him and the other child to be present, to show that I took this seriously.

But just as I was grabbing my keys, my email pinged. There was an urgent message from the advocacy group: a local incident of discrimination had just gone public, and they needed me to help organize a response, draft a statement, and speak to the press. The community was looking to me to stand up, to give voice to those who were hurt and ignored.

I felt torn in two. My child needed his mother, but the world needed an advocate. Both roles demanded my full attention, my heart, my voice. I stood in the hallway, keys in one hand, phone in the other, feeling the weight of both worlds pressing in, unsure which way to turn.
